turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Sorry we're late. The garage was a total mess, and he, uh, did not want to get out of the car.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, really. We were running behind too. Come sit.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Thanks. I'm on like my third coffee. He was up half the night.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. What brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): My right side. It started killing me in the night, and it goes down into my groin. It's like an eight, maybe a nine when it grabs, I don't know.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): That sounds miserable. When did it actually start?
[SEG0007] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He's been sore on and off since Sunday, so, err, about a week.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): No. That's not right. I was fine all week. It hit after midnight, just last night.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, so we've got about a week from you and last night from him. I'll leave it as somewhere between overnight and a week. Anything make it better or worse?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Walking makes it worse. Curling up does nothing. I'm tired of it.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does the pain stay in the side or move around?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): It moves. Right side down into the groin. I already said that.
[SEG0013] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He threw up in the bathroom, middle of the night. I heard him.
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Once. I threw up once. I can answer for myself.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Once still counts. Was there blood in the urine?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Pink at first, then it got darker. That part freaked me out.
[SEG0017] person_1 (CAREGIVER): The toilet looked red when I checked. Not a little pink.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any burning when you pee?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Just the blood, and the pain.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you still nauseous, or was it only that one time throwing up?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Still a bit queasy. Not like before.
[SEG0022] person_1 (CAREGIVER): He was shaking too, chills, when I got to him.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): I was not shaking. I didn't have chills. I was sweaty, that's all.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, you two don't agree on the chills, so I'm not going to decide that. Any trouble breathing, or pain in your chest?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your stomach otherwise, bowels, anything off there?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Bowels are fine.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines do you take?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Lisinopral. Umm, ten milligrams, every morning, for my blood pressure.
[SEG0030] person_1 (CAREGIVER): It's ten. I put it out every day and he doesn't miss it.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, we'll keep treating the high blood pressure. Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me read what the nurse wrote down, blood pressure one oh nine over seventy-seven. She had the pulse at ninety-six, uh no I misread that, it's eighty-four, and the temp is thirty-eight point three. Last time in March you were sixty-eight, that was the pulse then, and your last pressure was one-forty.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Sixty-eight sounds more like me. I feel awful.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): You do feel warm. Right loin is quite tender when I tap it. Belly is soft, and there's no guarding.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Ow. Yeah. That side. Can you not.

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to stamp a diagnosis on this yet. This could be a kidney stone, or it could be a kidney infection. Those are the two I'm holding, and I won't pick one till we look.
[SEG0038] person_1 (CAREGIVER): There's a urine dip stuck on the chart. The nurse said somebody should read it out.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Urine dip shows blood large, three plus. Leukocytes negative, nitrites negative.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): So what are you gonna do. I just want the pain gone.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm giving you a painkiller here today, ketorolac, thirty milligrams, a shot in the muscle. And I'm booking a CT of your abdomen and pelvis today, no contrast, to look for a stone.
[SEG0042] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Can he eat after that shot, or is that a bad idea?

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Light food is fine, and sip water if you can keep it down. If the pain gets unbearable or you can't pee, go to the ER. I'll see you back here this afternoon once the scan is read.

spec.situation: Sudden severe loin pain going to the groin overnight, vomiting once, blood in urine; pain score given loosely; urine dip result read aloud; painkiller and scan planned today.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Patient reports being sweaty, but transcript does not say it resolved.
Ketorolac 30 mg for pain is planned, but frequency 'once' is not explicitly stated.
bad.text: ketorolac (dose=30 mg, frequency=once, indication=pain, status=planned, reported_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Hematuria detail missing: patient said urine was pink at first then got darker; caregiver said the toilet looked red, not just a little pink.
